title: Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity
authors: Simon Martiel, Jay-U Chung, Alireza Seif, Soumik Ghosh, Ian Hincks, Abhinav Deshpande, Bill Fefferman, Jay M. Gambetta, Ali Javadi-Abhari
abstract: Sampling-based proposals are prominent candidates for demonstrating quantum computations beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, it has been difficult to combine their complexity-theoretic hardness with two capabilities needed for scalable quantum computing more generally: suppressing hardware errors, and verifying the quantum computation itself. Here we address both issues by introducing structured circuits, which, in addition to provable hardness guarantees, admit an encoding in a quantum code. This allows us to simultaneously reach high fidelities at high circuit depths, and to certify an experimental fidelity via the circuit structure and measurement of code syndromes. The resulting certificate is device dependent, but requires substantially weaker noise assumptions than existing fidelity proxy benchmarks. We demonstrate our proposal with a $70$-qubit, depth-$70$ Clifford circuit doped with $468$ $T$ gates. We use a total of $97$ physical qubits to encode this computation in spacetime codes, effectively suppressing gate error rates by $10\times$ after syndrome post-selection, and yielding a state with a fidelity lower bound of $0.284$ with $95\%$ confidence. Our construction is a systematic method for promoting a stabilizer state to a magic state while keeping an error-detected fidelity certificate.
summary: The paper presents a method called Doped Clifford Sampling (DCS) to demonstrate quantum computational hardness while simultaneously addressing hardware noise and verification. By encoding hard circuits into structured quantum codes, the authors achieve high fidelity at deep depths on superconducting qubits. This provides a systematic way to certify quantum advantage claims with quantifiable error bounds.
main_problem: The challenge is combining complexity-theoretic hardness (for quantum advantage) with the practical requirements of scalable quantum computation: error suppression and verifiable fidelity.
main_result: The authors propose a structured circuit approach that allows for high-fidelity sampling from hard quantum states while providing a device-dependent, quantifiable certificate of experimental fidelity.
method: They introduce 'structured circuits' encoded in quantum codes (spacetime codes) to simultaneously achieve hardness and error correction. Fidelity is certified by measuring code syndromes after syndrome post-selection.
model_or_system: The work uses a 70-qubit, depth-70 Clifford circuit doped with T gates, implemented on a superconducting quantum processor using 97 physical qubits for encoding in spacetime codes.
key_observables: Lower bound on the fidelity (e.g., $\ge 0.284$ at 95% confidence), syndrome measurement distributions, and the required number of physical qubits vs. logical qubits.
important_parameters: Circuit depth (70), number of T gates (468), encoding overhead (97 physical qubits for 70 data qubits), and fidelity lower bound ($\ge 0.284$).
main_assumptions: The resulting certificate is device dependent, and the fidelity lower bound relies on assuming a general Pauli noise model attainable by twirling gates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow of doped Clifford sampling (DCS), comparing measured vs. expected fidelities across doping stages; other figures detail qubit layouts and validation of the fidelity lower bound using DFE.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the DCS protocol, demonstrates its application to a large-scale circuit on superconducting hardware, quantifies the resulting fidelity lower bound through syndrome measurements, and compares this approach favorably against existing fidelity benchmarks.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the gap between theoretical quantum advantage claims (hardness) and experimental reality (noise/verification), providing a concrete framework for certifying computation in NISQ-era devices relevant to AMO platforms like trapped ions or superconducting circuits.

Figure 1 summarizes how the fidelity certificate is obtained in a DCS workflow. We begin with a ran- dom Clifford circuit, whose output state fidelity can be measured and verified efficiently using direct fidelity estimation (DFE) [20, 21]. Notably, DFE makes no assumptions about hardware noise. We then encode this circuit in a spacetime code, where post-selection on the zero syndrome projects the state into a low-error subspace [22]. Lastly, we increase the amount of non- Cliffordness (“magic”) by carefully doping with T gates while preserving the code structure. Figure 2. Constructing doped Clifford circuits within spacetime codes. a. A highly entangling Clif- ford circuit is encoded in a spacetime code and doped with T (Z-rotation) gates on wires not subject to X or Y error detection, producing an encoded state with high entanglement and magic. b. Additional ancillas improve error detection and fidelity at the cost of lower post-selection rates. Pauli-noise simulations agree well with experiment, assuming 0.1% CZ error, idle process fidelity e−t/τ with τ = 100 µs, and 0.3% readout error.

Figure 4. Validation of fidelity lower bound. a. Various doping counts (5, 75, 468) and types (T or S gates) are chosen that permit efficient measurement of fidelity (DFE) or fidelity proxy (XEB). XEB is known to overestimate fidelity due to readout errors, so we also show a rescaled quantity that controls for this effect. All experiments show that our estimated lower bound accurately captures the maximum loss in fidelity due to doping. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. b. Syndrome probability distributions show high consistency, regardless of doping strategy. This is consistent with a similar noise environment affecting all experiments, and doping gates being noiseless.
